label: 0B
title: Strings & Text
summary: String vs &str, creating and growing text, format!, bytes vs chars, slicing and its UTF-8 trap, trim/split/lines/replace/contains, parsing numbers, comparing, building text in loops, and reading stdin.

quest.title: Messages in Bottles
quest.story:
Every morning the lookout fishes bottles out of the sea. Each one holds a scrap of paper: orders, gossip, coordinates, and sometimes nonsense. The captain wants them decoded, cleaned up and logged, and you are the only deckhand who can read Rust.

Text is where many programs go wrong. Messages arrive with stray spaces, odd capitals and foreign letters like *ë* or *é*. Rust is strict about text: it is always valid UTF-8, a character can take several bytes, and the compiler won't let you pretend otherwise. That strictness pays off. Once your code compiles, it handles *Zoë* as well as *Zoe*.

Learn the two kinds of text, `String` and `&str`, and the dozen methods you'll use every day. Then decode the captain's bottle post and you're ready to keep the ledger in Level 1.

concepts.title: Two kinds of text: String and &str
concepts.body:
Rust has two everyday text types. Here's the mental model; Level 1 explains the rules behind it.

- **`String`** is text you **own**: a growable buffer, like your own notebook. You can append to it and change it (if the variable is `mut`). Build or store text in a `String`.
- **`&str`** ("string slice") is a **view** of text that lives somewhere else. String literals like `"ahoy"` are `&str`: their bytes are baked into the program. A `&str` can also look at all or part of a `String`.

```rust
let greeting: &str = "ahoy";                 // a literal: a view, read-only
let mut log: String = String::from("rum");   // owned and growable
log.push_str(", gold");
let view: &str = &log;                       // a view of the whole String
```

The everyday rule for functions:

```rust
fn shout(text: &str) -> String {      // read text: take &str
    format!("{}!", text.to_uppercase())   // new text: return String
}

shout("ahoy");          // a literal is already a &str
shout(&log);            // a String: lend it with &
```

Read the `&` as "let the function look at it". Why that matters, and what would happen without it, is the topic of Level 1.

concepts.title: Making and growing Strings
concepts.body:
```rust
let a = String::from("gold");     // from a literal
let b = "rum".to_string();        // same thing
let mut c = String::new();        // empty
c.push('x');                      // push ONE char (single quotes)
c.push_str("yz");                 // push a &str (double quotes)
c += "!";                         // also appends a &str
let d = format!("{a} and {b}");   // "gold and rum": the usual way to combine
let e: &str = d.as_str();         // a &str view of a String (same as &d)
```

`+` works too, but it **uses up** the left `String`: `let s = a + "-" + &b;` leaves `a` unusable afterwards. Level 1 calls this a *move*. Until then, prefer `format!` for combining. It never uses anything up.

Methods like `to_uppercase()`, `trim()` and `replace()` never change the original text. `to_uppercase` and `replace` return a **new** `String`, and `trim` returns a `&str` view:

```rust
let loud = d.to_uppercase();   // d is unchanged
```

concepts.title: Length, bytes and chars
concepts.body:
Rust text is **UTF-8**. ASCII letters take 1 byte, but `é` takes 2 bytes, `€` 3 and `🦀` 4. `len()` counts **bytes**, not characters:

```rust
let word = "café";
word.len();             // 5 bytes
word.chars().count();   // 4 chars
```

Walk the characters with `.chars()` and the raw bytes with `.bytes()`:

```rust
for c in "Zoë".chars() {        // 'Z', 'o', 'ë'
    if c.is_alphabetic() { /* … */ }
}
```

Handy `char` methods: `is_alphabetic()`, `is_ascii_digit()`, `is_whitespace()`, `is_uppercase()`, `to_ascii_uppercase()`, `to_ascii_lowercase()`. `c.to_uppercase()` also exists, but because some letters become two characters (`ß` → `SS`) it returns several chars. Push them with `out.extend(c.to_uppercase())`.

To get the first character: `s.chars().next()`. It gives `Some(c)`, or `None` for empty text (more on that below).

concepts.title: Slicing &s[a..b] and the UTF-8 trap
Searching, trimming and transforming
concepts.body:
All of these leave the original untouched:

```rust
let s = "  Black Pearl  ";
s.trim();                      // "Black Pearl" (also trim_start, trim_end)
s.contains("Pearl");           // true
s.trim().starts_with("Black"); // true (and ends_with)
s.find('P');                   // Some(8): byte position, or None
s.replace("Pearl", "Gull");    // a new String
s.to_lowercase();              // a new String
"ab".repeat(3);                // "ababab"
```

Splitting gives you the pieces one by one. Use them in a `for` loop, or count them:

```rust
for word in "rum  and gold".split_whitespace() { }   // "rum", "and", "gold"
for part in "a,b,,c".split(',') { }                  // "a", "b", "", "c"
for line in text.lines() { }                         // one line at a time
let n = text.lines().count();
let (key, value) = "gold=30".split_once('=').unwrap(); // ("gold", "30")
```

`split_once` gives `Some((before, after))`, or `None` if the separator is missing. 0C shows how to collect pieces into a list with `.collect()`.

concepts.title: Numbers from text, Option, and comparing
concepts.body:
`parse` turns text into a number, but it can fail, so it gives a `Result`: either `Ok(number)` or `Err(problem)`.

```rust
let n: u32 = "42".parse().unwrap();            // 42; panics on bad input
let m: u32 = "x7".trim().parse().unwrap_or(0); // 0: a fallback instead of a panic
if let Ok(k) = " 12 ".trim().parse::<u32>() {  // only runs on success
    println!("got {k}");
}
```

Methods that may find nothing, like `find`, `split_once` and `chars().next()`, give an `Option`: `Some(value)` or `None`. They use the same tools: `unwrap_or(…)`, `if let Some(x) = …`, or a `match`:

```rust
match line.split_once(':') {
    Some((name, amount)) => println!("{name} = {amount}"),
    None => println!("not a pair"),
}
```

`unwrap()` means "I'm sure it's there; panic if not". Level 5 is all about `Option`, `Result` and doing this properly. Always `trim()` before `parse()`: `" 42".parse::<u32>()` fails.

Comparing: `==` works between `String` and `&str` in both directions. Comparison is exact and case-sensitive (`"Rum" != "rum"`); use `a.eq_ignore_ascii_case(b)` or lowercase both sides. `<` compares byte by byte, so all capitals sort before all lowercase letters: `"Zebra" < "apple"`.

concepts.title: Building text in a loop, and reading input

steps.note: A literal is a &str: a pointer and a length (4). The bytes are baked into the program, not the heap.
String::from copies the text into a heap buffer that log owns: pointer, length, capacity.
push_str grows the buffer. Here it was too small, so a bigger one was allocated.
&log[0..3] is a view of bytes 0..3 of log's buffer. Nothing is copied.
to_uppercase builds a brand-new String. log itself is unchanged.
End of main: each String frees its own buffer. Views and literals free nothing.

challenges.title: How long is a café?
challenges.story: A bottle from a French port. The lookout measures the message and gets two different answers.
hints: `len()` and `chars().count()` measure different things. Which one counts bytes?
In UTF-8, `é` needs two bytes. And does `to_uppercase()` change `word`, or return something new?
5 bytes, 4 chars. `to_uppercase` returns a new `String`, so `word` still prints in lowercase.

challenges.title: Half a letter
challenges.story: The lookout wants the first three letters of a sailor's name for the duty roster.
challenges.prompt: What happens when you compile and run this program?
hints: Slice ranges are **byte** positions. How many bytes do `Z`, `o` and `ë` take?
`Z` and `o` take one byte each, and `ë` takes two. Where does byte 3 fall?
Byte 3 is in the middle of `ë`. Slicing there can't be checked at compile time, so it panics at runtime: "byte index 3 is not a char boundary".

choices.label: Compile error E0277: a `str` can't be indexed
It compiles, but panics at runtime

challenges.title: Fix the greeting
challenges.story: The bosun's greeting program mixes up its kinds of text. *Rustc* lists three complaints.
challenges.prompt:
Make the program compile and print exactly:

```text
Ahoy! Ferris (F)
```

Rules:
- `greeting` stays a `String` (keep the `: String` annotation).
- Take the initial from `name` with `chars()`. Don't type a literal `F`.
- Keep the `println!` line as it is.
hints: Three errors, three different mix-ups: a `&str` where a `String` is expected, a `char` where a `&str` is expected, and indexing into text.

A literal is a `&str`. Turn it into a `String` with `String::from(…)` or `.to_string()`. `push_str` takes text in double quotes, and `push` takes one `char` in single quotes. Text can't be indexed with `[0]` (E0277).
`String::from("Ahoy")`, `greeting.push('!')` (or `push_str("!")`), and `name.chars().next().unwrap()` for the first character.

require.message: Take the initial with chars(), as the rules say.

forbid.message: Don't type the initial: take it from name.

challenges.title: Signal flags
challenges.story: The signal officer needs three small text tools before the next ship comes into view.
challenges.prompt:
Implement the three functions. Each takes a `&str` and returns new text or a number:

- `fn shout(s: &str) -> String`: trim the spaces at both ends, uppercase it, add `!`. `"  ahoy there "` → `"AHOY THERE!"`. Empty or blank input gives just `"!"`.
- `fn count_vowels(s: &str) -> usize`: how many of the **characters** are one of `a e i o u`, upper or lower case. `"Pearl"` → 2.
- `fn initials(name: &str) -> String`: the first character of every word (words are separated by any whitespace), uppercased. `"anne  bonny"` → `"AB"`, `""` → `""`.

Hidden tests call all three functions directly.
hints: `shout` is one line: chain `trim()` and `to_uppercase()` inside a `format!`. The other two walk the text: `for c in s.chars()` and `for word in name.split_whitespace()`.
For vowels, lowercase each char with `c.to_ascii_lowercase()` and `match` it against `'a' | 'e' | 'i' | 'o' | 'u'`. For initials, `word.chars().next()` gives `Some(first_char)`.
`format!("{}!", s.trim().to_uppercase())`. Initials: `let mut out = String::new(); for word in name.split_whitespace() { if let Some(c) = word.chars().next() { out.extend(c.to_uppercase()); } } out`.

challenges.title: Rum, rum and RUM
challenges.story: The quartermaster compares cargo names, and his program's answers surprise him.
hints: Can a `String` be compared with a `&str` at all? (Yes. Both sides hold text.) Is the comparison case-sensitive?
`to_lowercase()` returns a new `String` with the same letters in lowercase. `<` compares strings byte by byte, and every uppercase ASCII letter has a smaller byte value than every lowercase one.
`"Rum" == "rum"` is false, `"rum" == "rum"` is true, and `'Z'` (90) comes before `'a'` (97), so `"Zebra" < "apple"` is true.

choices.label: Compile error E0277: can't compare `String` with `&str`

challenges.title: The purser's tally
challenges.story: Bottles from the supply ships carry lists like `rum: 12`. Some lines are smudged.
challenges.prompt:
Implement the three functions:

- `fn parse_amount(s: &str) -> u32`: the number in `s`, ignoring surrounding spaces. If it isn't a valid `u32`, return `0`. `" 12 "` → 12, `"x"` → 0.
- `fn tally(text: &str) -> u32`: `text` has one entry per line in the form `name: amount`. Return the sum of all amounts. Lines without a `:` count as 0, and so do lines whose amount doesn't parse.
- `fn tidy(s: &str) -> String`: collapse every run of whitespace into a single space and remove leading and trailing whitespace. `"  rum   and\tgold "` → `"rum and gold"`.

Hidden tests call all three.
hints: `parse` gives a `Result`. Which method turns it into a plain number with a fallback? And what must you do to `" 12 "` before parsing?

In `tally`, loop over `text.lines()`, and use `split_once(':')` to split each line into name and amount. It gives an `Option`, so use `if let Some((name, amount)) = …`. Reuse `parse_amount`. For `tidy`, `split_whitespace()` already ignores runs of spaces and tabs.
`s.trim().parse().unwrap_or(0)`. In `tidy`, push a `' '` before every word except the first: `if !out.is_empty() { out.push(' '); } out.push_str(word);`.

challenges.title: Names on the roster
challenges.story: The roster is a mess: `jACK sparrow`, `ANNE bonny`. The captain wants it tidy, and he wants to know which names read the same backwards.
challenges.prompt:
Write two functions:

- `fn title_case(s: &str) -> String`: every word gets an uppercase first letter and lowercase for the rest, and words are separated by single spaces. `"jACK   sparrow"` → `"Jack Sparrow"`, `"émile"` → `"Émile"`, `""` → `""`.
- `fn is_palindrome(s: &str) -> bool`: `true` if the **letters and digits** of `s`, compared case-insensitively, read the same forwards and backwards. Everything else (spaces, punctuation) is ignored. `"Never odd or even"` → `true`, `"Rum"` → `false`, `""` → `true`.

Keep a `fn main()`; it can print something or stay empty. Hidden tests call both. After they pass, the tutor judges whether your solution is idiomatic.
challenges.starter:
// Write title_case(s: &str) -> String and is_palindrome(s: &str) -> bool here.

fn main() {}
hints: `title_case` is the "build text in a loop" pattern over `split_whitespace()`. For each word, treat the first char and the rest separately.

`let mut chars = word.chars();` then `chars.next()` takes the first char, and `chars.as_str()` is the rest of the word as a `&str`. For the palindrome, first build a `String` with only the lowercased letters and digits (`c.is_alphanumeric()`).
Reverse text by its chars: `let reversed: String = letters.chars().rev().collect();`, then compare with `==`. Never reverse bytes: that breaks multi-byte letters.
challenges.rubric: Idiomatic beginner text handling: parameters are `&str`, results are new `String`s. Words come from `split_whitespace()`, characters from `chars()`, never from byte indexes or `as u8` arithmetic, so non-ASCII letters work. Uppercasing uses `to_uppercase()`/`to_lowercase()` (or the char versions with `extend`), not hand-made ASCII tables. Building output uses `String::new()` plus `push`/`push_str`, or iterator `collect`/`join`; either is fine. The palindrome compares chars (e.g. a filtered lowercase `String` against its `chars().rev()`), not bytes. Deduct for slicing with computed byte offsets (`&word[1..]` is acceptable only because the first char's length is known via `chars()`/`char::len_utf8`), unnecessary `.to_string()`/`String::from` copies in loops, or `unwrap()` on values that can be empty.

challenges.title: Boss: Bottle post
challenges.story: A whole crate of bottles washed up overnight. The captain wants every message decoded before breakfast, and the lookout has already copied them into one long text.
challenges.prompt:
Write the decoder. The program reads **all of stdin** and handles it line by line:

1. Trim the line. Skip it if it is empty or starts with `#` (a comment).
2. Every other line is a message. A message looks like `verb: text`: split at the **first** `:`, then trim both parts. The verb is case-insensitive (`SHOUT`, `Shout`).
3. Print one output line per message:
   - `shout` → the text uppercased, followed by `!`
   - `whisper` → the text lowercased, followed by `...`
   - `reverse` → the text with its **characters** in reverse order
   - `count` → `N words, M chars`, where words are separated by whitespace and chars are characters (not bytes) of the trimmed text
   - anything else, or a line without `:` → `?? ` followed by the trimmed line
4. Finally print `decoded X of Y messages`, where Y counts every message and X counts those that were not `??`.

For this input:

```text
# from the Black Pearl
shout: ahoy there
whisper: The MAP is FAKE

reverse: Zoë
count: rum  and   gold
dance: jig
no colon here
```

the output is exactly:

```text
AHOY THERE!
the map is fake...
ëoZ
3 words, 15 chars
?? dance: jig
?? no colon here
decoded 4 of 6 messages
```

The hidden cases include empty input, padded and uppercase verbs, and non-ASCII text. Use the **stdin** box next to Run to try your own input.
hints: Split the work. `main` does the loop: `for line in text.lines()`, shadow `let line = line.trim();`, `continue` for blanks and comments, and count. `decode` handles a single message and returns the output line.

`line.split_once(':')` gives `Some((verb, text))` or `None`. For a case-insensitive verb, lowercase it and compare it, or `match` on `verb.trim().to_lowercase().as_str()` (a `match` on text needs a `&str`, which is what `as_str()` gives).

`reverse` must reverse **chars**: `text.chars().rev().collect::<String>()`. `count`: `text.split_whitespace().count()` words and `text.chars().count()` chars. Track `total` and `decoded` with two `mut` counters in `main`.

One shape for `decode`: `match line.split_once(':') { None => format!("?? {line}"), Some((verb, text)) => { let text = text.trim(); match verb.trim().to_lowercase().as_str() { "shout" => format!("{}!", text.to_uppercase()), /* … */ _ => format!("?? {line}") } } }`.

cards.front: `String` vs `&str`: which is which, and which do you use for a function parameter that only reads text?
cards.back: `String` is owned, growable text (a heap buffer). `&str` is a view of text that lives elsewhere: a literal or part of a `String`. Read-only parameters take `&str`. Pass a literal directly, or a `String` as `&s`. Return new text as `String`.
`5` vs `4`. `len()` counts **bytes** of UTF-8, and `é` takes two. Count characters with `chars().count()`.

cards.front: After `let loud = word.to_uppercase();`, what is in `word`?
cards.back: The original text, unchanged. `to_uppercase`, `to_lowercase`, `replace` and `trim` never modify the original. They return a new `String` (`trim` returns a `&str` view).
It **panics** at runtime: "byte index 3 is not a char boundary". Slice ranges are byte positions, and `ë` occupies bytes 2–3. Let `find`/`split`/`chars` find positions for you.

cards.front: Why doesn't `name[0]` compile for a `&str`, and how do you get the first character?
cards.back: E0277: `str` can't be indexed by an integer, because a byte might be half a character. Use `name.chars().next()`, which gives `Some(c)`, or `None` for empty text.
`push('!')` appends one `char` (single quotes). `push_str("!!")` appends a `&str` (double quotes). `s += "x"` also appends a `&str`. To combine several values, `format!` is usually clearest.

`false`: `==` works between `String` and `&str`, but it's case-sensitive. `true`: `<` compares bytes, and uppercase ASCII letters come before lowercase ones. Lowercase both sides, or use `eq_ignore_ascii_case`, for case-insensitive comparison.

cards.front: How do you turn `" 42 "` into a `u32`, falling back to 0 for bad input?
cards.back: `s.trim().parse::<u32>().unwrap_or(0)`. `parse` returns a `Result` (`Ok(n)` or `Err(e)`), and without `trim()` the spaces make it fail. `.unwrap()` would panic instead of falling back.
`Some(("gold", " 30"))`: the parts before and after the first `:`, untrimmed. For `"gold"`, `None`. Handle both with `if let Some((k, v)) = …` or `match`.

cards.front: How do you reverse a string correctly?
cards.back: By characters: `s.chars().rev().collect::<String>()`. Reversing bytes would break multi-byte characters like `ë`.

cards.front: The recipe to read all of stdin into a `String`?
cards.back: `use std::io::{self, Read};` then `let mut text = String::new(); io::stdin().read_to_string(&mut text).unwrap();`, and `for line in text.lines() { … }`.
